[Message by unknown at bfd4c472-c7aa-551b-b226-15026bd006f5]
I am an experienced hiring manager and have worked with many recruiters.  I would like to dispel a myth.  ATS does NOT pick resumes.  At least in the US, all resumes must be reviewed by a human.  ATS can  be used to assist the human in finding keywords, which are mostly specific technical words like "Python" or "Salesforce".  ATS are NOT used to match words like "team player".   There is a lot of misinformation from people who don't know how things work or from companies trying to sell snake oil with "ATS compliant" resumes.  THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS "ATS compliant"!  Hope that helps.

[Message by unknown at beba30fa-6486-5816-b23f-705168b016b6]
Hi there everyone — I am thinking through common LLM capabilities that are most often used when creating AI-enabled features in software apps.  I know every software app, esp. enterprise software, have their own requirements and features to support users.  But in the end, I have a sense that many of those features that leverage AI are actually rather similar when distilled down.

Here’s my list so far:

• *Data extraction*: Capturing from unstructured text into a object (e.g. JSON object) using a template/schema
• *Spam or malicious content detection*
• *Summarize (reduction):* Reducing a larger set of text into a content that highlights the key points.
• *Explanation*: Rephrase input text address a selected audience while remaining accurate; may include summarization, though required.
• *Content Tagging*: Apply tags for text using predefined tags, and/or define new tags based on configured criteria.
• *Content Translation*: Translate content into another language(s)
• *Sentiment*:  Similar to tagging, primarily looking at the style + tonality of the input text versus the factual content itself.
Do these represent what your AI features address? What am I missing?

Developed a framework for deciding what operations to integrate AI into. Thought I'd share it here. You can learn more in our free lightning lesson coming up this Friday: <https://maven.com/p/3cb375/how-to-build-an-agent-native-workplace>

Here's a framework for identifying where generative AI actually drives value:
1. Map your current operations with surgical precision. Decompose each workflow into granular tasks. Surface every implicit decision point in your processes.
2. Evaluate each micro-task individually. Deploy traditional software when:
- The process follows identical steps every time
- Accuracy is mission-critical
- Speed and efficiency trump creative variation
- You're integrating with established enterprise systems

DON'T USE AI

Deploy generative AI when:
- No existing software solution addresses the challenge
- You're processing unstructured human language or messy datasets
- Creative interpretation creates competitive advantage
- Near-perfect accuracy is acceptable (not mandatory)

Maybe your traditional software isn't perfect. But at least its predictable. It's an old friend whom you accepted with all the quirks and flaws. You know what you're getting into.

Generative AI applications are unpredictable by design. There is no bug to fix and sleep soundly. Everything is a statistical game. The winning mindset is: don't start playing that game unless you really have to.

I’ve been thinking a lot about *learning loops...* not the big formal ones (like quarterly health surveys or sprint retros), but the small, informal ones that happen in the flow of work.

The kind where you:
• Ask a quick gut-check in Slack
• Debrief for 5 minutes after a meeting
• Share a rough draft and ask, “What’s missing or confusing?”
These *little loops* have been a game-changer for catching friction early and making systems actually stick especially in Product Ops work.

The most counter-intuitive thing about requirements is that worse is actually better.

Let that sink in.

As Product Managers we usually aim for exactly the opposite. We endlessly rewrite and polish our requirements, trying to chase perfection.

Every draft, tweak and fine-tune brings us closer to feeling proud. We carefully weigh and scrutinize every word before presenting our pristine requirements to the team.

When we finally lay out all the requirements to the team, everybody is quiet. We get zero questions and we pat ourselves on the shoulders for a job well done.

They ask zero questions, because everything is perfectly clear, right?

WRONG!

This kind of diligence is the biggest mistake you can make when formulating requirements. All this effort usually ends up in disaster by making our requirements worse in ways that are nearly impossible to detect and fix.

Why does trying to make our requirements better usually end up making them worse?

Why are gold-plated requirements worse than shoddy requirements?

How can we prevent the effort spent on formulating good requirements from backfiring?

Let’s dig in together!

This is an updated post on PLG onboarding call. One thing I've recognized is that we've spoken to a lot of our competitor's churned users, and what we found is that they engaged because of the promise of the product and what it could deliver. However, when it came to actual usage, it failed to deliver.

It's not the technology that's the issue; it's often the activation and onboarding process. Users may not be fully guided to set up the product, or it's unclear what the product is actually doing. As a result, they're not taking full advantage of its capabilities.

That's why it's so important to ensure users are activating and are fully aware of the value. This can only be achieved by having calls with customers and understanding where they struggle, what's not obvious, and what's blocking them from moving forward.

We're investing in this as a continuous process, but I believe every company needs to invest six months to one year on this for founders to truly understand the problem, pain points, solution, and product fit for their customers.

We learned through onboarding how people are. They share their process with us, share their screens, and let us know what's bothering them. They tell us what urgent pain they need a solution for and what was just an unrealistic expectation as well.

Without actually doing a call, you'll never know. On top of that, you'll never know how to price the product appropriately because you just don't know where it fits.

I'm happy to go deeper into this because I truly believe in the value of an onboarding call. It's the ultimate lever to solve your product pricing and growth challenges.

Virality Explained

Internal Virality (Bottom-Up Adoption)
• Tally: Teams co-create forms, inviting coworkers and spreading use across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes helps more teammates join and participate.
• Slack: One invite leads to many, with team chats spreading company-wide.
• 
External Virality (New Users)
• Shortwave: External recipients of shared emails or summaries are prompted to try the product.
• Tally.so: Shared forms display Tally branding, encouraging external sign-ups.
• Asana: Task or project invites brought in external partners, expanding user base.
Viral SaaS Product Characteristics
• User-Driven Value Sharing: Product gets better as users interact/share.
• Network-Enabled Use Cases: Value increases with a connected user base.
• Built-In Triggers: Features like “invite” or “share” prompt engagement.
• Fast, Simple Onboarding: New users get up to speed and see value immediately.
• Leverages Existing Networks: Designed to help users invite their contacts.
Read more on the tactics to implement viral SaaS using Product Led Growth <https://growthwithgary.com/p/saas-virality>

Ever heard of a “reverse trial” for SaaS?
Most folks know about free trials (use all the features for a week, then pay or get locked out) and freemium (use basic features for free forever). But a reverse trial flips things around for better results.

Here’s how it works:
New users start with full premium access, right away! After 7 or 30 days, if they don’t pay, they aren’t kicked out. Instead, they move to a free plan with some limits, but can still use the product and keep their work.

Why does this help?
Old way: About 15% pay after a free trial. The rest usually leave and don’t come back.
vs.
Reverse trial: 15% pay, but another 25% stick around on the free plan, which means you keep up to 40% of all signups using your tool and thinking about upgrading later.

So, instead of losing most of your trial users, you keep them close... giving them more chances to upgrade when the time is right.

<https://growthwithgary.com/p/reverse-trial>

Get my SaaS to "Go Viral"

How Tally.so, <http://Granola.ai|Granola.ai>, Shortwave, Slack, and Asana STACKING growth with bottom-up product-led strategies and built-in virality.

*Internal virality (bottom-up adoption)*
• Tally: Teams collaborate on forms and templates, inviting coworkers to co-create and review, spreading usage across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes and summaries inside the company encourages more teammates to join and access shared knowledge.
• Slack: One person invites teammates to a channel, and soon the whole company is chatting and collaborating in real time.
*External virality (net new users)*
• Shortwave: When users send collaborative email threads or magic summaries, recipients outside the company experience the product and are prompted to try it themselves. 
• Tally.so: Every form shared externally carries Tally branding, exposing new users and making it easy for them to sign up and create their own forms. 
• Asana: Task assignments and project invites sent to external partners or clients introduce them to the platform, driving new sign-ups beyond the original organization.
*What are the Characteristics of a Viral SaaS Product?*
1. User-Driven Value Sharing - The product becomes more valuable as users interact or collaborate with others, making sharing a natural part of the workflow.
2. Network-Enabled Use Cases - The product improves when users connect with colleagues, customers, and friends who benefit from having a shared knowledge base.
3. Built-In Triggers - The product with “invite,” “share,” or “assign” artifact motivates new users to engage.
4. Fast, Simple Onboarding- New users can get started and see the value quickly, no complicated setup.
5. Uses Your Existing Network - The product is made to help you invite people you already know, so it spreads faster.
Read more on the tactics to implement viral SaaS using Product Led Growth <https://growthwithgary.com/p/saas-virality>
